concepts.title: Costs and taxes
concepts.summary: Think in all-in cost, not just the sticker fee; know what distributions are and how tax lots work; and put each asset in the account type where the tax code punishes it least — location can be worth more than fund selection.

cards.h: All-in cost
cards.md:
The expense ratio is the sticker price. What you actually pay to own a fund is the **all-in cost**:

- **Expense ratio** — charged per year of holding
- **Bid-ask spread** — charged per round trip
- **Tracking difference beyond the fee** — sloppy indexing leaks return invisibly
- **Taxes** — on distributions each year, and on your gains when you sell

The useful insight is that these scale with *different things*. Holding costs scale with **time**; trading costs scale with **activity**; taxes scale with both, plus account type. So the cheapest possible setup is no accident: broad low-fee ETFs (tiny ratio, penny spreads, near-zero capital-gains distributions), traded rarely, in the right account. Each term in the cost equation gets minimized by the same boring behavior.

And the sticker can mislead in both directions: a 0.03% fund traded weekly can cost more than a 0.20% fund held for a decade. For an ETF investor, *activity itself* is a cost center — remember that when concept 7's temptations show up.

cards.h: Distributions and tax lots
cards.md:
Two pieces of plumbing every taxable-account investor should know.

**Distributions.** Funds pass through what they collect. Stock ETFs pay **dividends** (typically quarterly); most broad-ETF dividends are *qualified*, taxed at the lower capital-gains rates rather than as ordinary income. Bond fund interest is generally taxed as **ordinary income** — at your full marginal rate; remember that for the next card. Capital-gains distributions, the mutual-fund December surprise from concept 1, are rare in broad ETFs. Note that reinvesting a distribution doesn't dodge the tax — it's taxable the year it's paid, reinvested or not.

**Tax lots.** Every separate purchase you make is a **lot** with its own price paid (**cost basis**) and its own clock. Sell after holding a lot more than a year and the gain is **long-term** — taxed at favorable rates (0/15/20%). A year or less is **short-term** — taxed like salary. The clock alone can change the tax on the same gain by a third or more.

When you sell *part* of a position, your broker's default is often "first in, first out" — usually your oldest, cheapest, biggest-gain shares. But you can elect **specific identification** and choose which lots to sell: pick high-basis lots to shrink the taxable gain, or harvest a losing lot to offset gains elsewhere. Same sale, same proceeds, different tax bill — set the cost-basis method in your account settings *before* you need it.

cards.h: Asset location: the free lunch nobody eats
cards.md:
You likely have accounts with different tax treatment: **taxable** brokerage, **tax-deferred** (401(k), traditional IRA (Individual Retirement Account) — pay ordinary income tax on the way out), and **tax-free** (Roth — never taxed again). **Asset location** is the art of placing each asset where the tax code hurts it least. Same portfolio, same funds, same risk — measurably more money kept.

The logic follows directly from the last card. Ask of each asset: *how heavily is its return taxed each year?*

- **Taxable bonds and REITs** (Real Estate Investment Trusts) throw off income taxed at full ordinary rates, every single year. In a taxable account that's a steady leak; **shelter them** in tax-advantaged accounts where the annual tax simply doesn't happen.
- **Broad stock ETFs** are already nearly tax-optimal: qualified dividends at low rates, capital gains deferred until *you* choose to sell (thanks to the wrapper from concept 1). They **tolerate a taxable account** better than almost anything else you could put there.
- **Highest-expected-growth assets** have a natural home in the **Roth**, where all that growth escapes tax entirely.

Studies of the taxable-vs-sheltered decision typically put the benefit in the range of **0.1–0.3% per year** — comparable to the entire fee difference between a cheap fund and an expensive one, earned not by picking anything better but purely by *placement*. Most investors agonize over which fund and never think about which account. This card is the cheaper worry.

questions.prompt: Which cost do you pay every time you trade, regardless of how long you've held?
options: The expense ratio
The bid-ask spread
Capital gains distributions
The gross-to-net fee waiver
feedback: The expense ratio accrues with time held — it's the rent, not the toll; trading more doesn't raise it.
Right — the spread is charged per transaction, which is exactly why activity itself is a cost center for an ETF investor.
Distributions arrive on the fund's schedule whether you trade or not — they scale with holding, not with trading.
The waiver is a discount on the expense ratio, not a per-trade charge — it affects the rent, not the toll.

questions.prompt: You hold taxable bond funds and broad stock ETFs, plus both a taxable account and an IRA. The tax-smart arrangement is:
options: Bonds in taxable, stocks in the IRA
Bonds in the IRA, stock ETFs in taxable — bond interest is taxed annually at ordinary rates and needs shelter; stock ETFs defer gains and pay lower-taxed dividends
Split everything 50/50 across both accounts
It makes no difference where anything goes
feedback: Backwards — this parks the heavily-taxed annual income stream in the taxed account and shelters the asset that barely needed it.
Right — shelter what leaks (ordinary-income interest, every year), expose what's naturally tax-efficient (deferred gains, qualified dividends). Same portfolio, more kept.
Splitting evenly forfeits the choice entirely — location only adds value when assets are deliberately sorted by tax burden.
Placement is typically worth 0.1–0.3% per year — on par with the whole cheap-vs-expensive fund fee gap, for zero change in risk.

questions.prompt: You bought shares of the same ETF in 2019 (at $100) and last month (at $195). Price today: $200. You need to sell some shares while minimizing this year's tax bill. You should:
options: Let the broker's default pick the shares — it's all the same
Use specific identification to sell last month's $195-basis lot — a $5/share gain instead of $100/share
Sell the 2019 lot because older shares are always taxed less
Sell everything to keep the bookkeeping simple
feedback: Defaults are often first-in-first-out, which here sells the $100-basis lot and books twenty times the gain — the default is the expensive choice.

Right — same shares sold, same cash raised, $5 of taxable gain per share instead of $100. (Check the fine print: gains on lots held under a year are short-term, but $5 short-term beats $100 long-term here by a mile.)
Older lots get the long-term *rate*, but the rate applies to a $100 gain — the lot's basis matters more than its birthday in this case.
Selling everything realizes the full gain on every lot at once — maximum possible tax bill, purchased for a tidier spreadsheet.

questions.prompt: You have dividends automatically reinvested. Are they still taxed in a taxable account?
options: No — reinvested dividends aren't income
Yes — a distribution is taxable the year it's paid, whether you pocket it or reinvest it; the reinvestment just creates a new tax lot
Only if the fund's price also went up that year
Only when you eventually sell the fund
feedback: The IRS sees the dividend the moment it's paid — what you do next (spend or reinvest) doesn't change its character as income.
Right — and that new lot has its own basis and clock, which is why long-held reinvesting positions accumulate dozens of lots. Brokers track this, but the specific-ID option is yours.
Dividend taxation is independent of price movement — a fund can fall all year and its dividends are still taxable income.
That's how capital *gains* on your shares work — dividends are taxed on arrival, not at sale.

concepts.title: How investors actually lose
concepts.summary: The expensive ETF mistakes are behavioral, not technical: chasing last year's winner, treating theme funds as lottery tickets, over-trading, mistaking overlap for diversification, and selling in the middle of a crash.

cards.h: Performance chasing and the behavior gap
cards.md:
The most reliable finding in fund-investor research is embarrassing in its simplicity: **investors earn less than the funds they invest in.**

How can that be? Timing of the money. A fund posts a hot three-year run; money floods in *after* the gains are already banked; the hot streak cools (as hot streaks statistically do — that's what made them streaks); money flees near the bottom. The fund's posted return counts the whole ride. The average *dollar* only showed up for the ending. Morningstar's long-running "Mind the Gap" studies put this **behavior gap** around one percentage point per year — for many investors, bigger than every fee, spread, and tax drag combined. The killer detail: the gap is *widest* in the most exciting, volatile funds, because exciting funds are the ones that get bought high and sold low.

The mechanism to internalize: a stellar recent record mostly tells you a fund's holdings just got *more expensive*, not that they're about to repeat. Past performance isn't just a weak signal — buying it systematically puts your dollars in *after* the returns happened. Buy the boring plan, automate the contributions, and the gap mostly closes by itself.

cards.h: Lottery tickets and busy hands
cards.md:
**Theme funds.** Every hype cycle mints ETFs to match — genomics, robotics, cannabis, blockchain, AI (Artificial Intelligence). Here's the structural problem, beyond mere fashion: a theme ETF launches *when the theme can sell*, which is at or near **peak excitement** — after the story is famous and the stocks are already expensive. Research on thematic funds finds exactly what that predicts: on average they underperform badly *after* launch, whatever the theme later achieves in the real world. The theme can change the world and the fund can still lose money — because the price you paid had the world-changing already in it. A fund launch is a measure of what's sellable, never of what's cheap.

**Over-trading.** ETFs trade in one click, and the click is the trap. Every trade pays the spread; every profitable sale in a taxable account books a tax bill (short-term rates if you're quick, per concept 6); and every trade is a fresh chance for the timing errors of the last card. Decades of brokerage-account research agree: **the more retail investors trade, the worse they do** — the famous study title is simply "Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth." The ETF's greatest convenience, always-on tradability, is thus its subtlest hazard: the instrument is liquid, but your *plan* shouldn't be. Activity feels like diligence; in investing it's usually leakage. When the itch strikes, size it like a satellite: small enough that being wrong doesn't matter.

cards.h: The one mistake that ends compounding
cards.md:
Cheap funds, clean diversification, tax-smart placement — one act can undo a decade of all of it: **selling in the middle of a crash**.

The market's rhythm is brutal on this specific plan: its **best days cluster tightly around its worst days**, because rebounds are born in the depths of panics. So "sell now, get back in when things calm down" doesn't sidestep the crash — it locks in the losses, then *specifically* misses the violent rebound days, because by the time things feel calm, the snapback already happened. Miss a small handful of those days over a few decades and a huge slice of the total return is gone. The people who caught them weren't nimble; they were simply **still there** — the strategy known, only half-jokingly, as staying in your seat.

Two defenses, both built in advance:

- **Set your stock/bond mix by the crash, not the average year.** Decide what drop you could watch without selling — then size stocks so the plausible worst case stays inside that line. The mix you can hold through a panic beats the optimal mix you'll abandon in one, by exactly the amount the panic costs.
- **Write the plan down in peacetime** — target mix, when you rebalance, what you'll do in a 30% drawdown (spoiler: mostly nothing, perhaps rebalance *into* the drop). In a crash you don't want to be deciding; you want to be *complying* with a decision made by the calmer person you were.

Every concept in this pack compounds only if you stay invested. Protecting against the big, permanent loss — including the self-inflicted kind — *is* the strategy.

questions.prompt: The "behavior gap" — investors earning about 1% per year less than their own funds — is caused by:
options: Fund companies skimming returns secretly
The timing of investors' money: it arrives after the gains and leaves near the bottoms, so the average dollar misses the posted return
Government taxes on fund investors
Rounding errors in fund accounting
feedback: Fees are disclosed and already deducted from the fund return — the gap is measured *after* fees, in the investor's own timing.
Right — the fund's return counts the whole ride; chasing dollars only show up for the ending. The gap is widest in the most exciting funds, which is a hint about what to own.
Taxes are real but separate — the gap appears even in tax-sheltered accounts, purely from buy-high/sell-low flow timing.
Fund accounting is audited to the penny — the leak is in investor behavior, which no audit can fix.

questions.prompt: Why do thematic ETFs (AI, robotics, genomics...) tend to disappoint even when the underlying technology succeeds?
options: The technologies always fail
They launch when hype — and the stocks' prices — peak, because that's when the fund can sell; the world-changing future is already in the purchase price
Theme funds are illegal in most states
They hold no actual stocks
feedback: Many themed technologies succeed spectacularly — the fund can still lose money because success was pre-paid in the entry price.
Right — launch timing follows salability, and salability peaks with hype. You can be exactly right about the future and still overpay for it today.
They're fully legal and heavily marketed — the problem is economics, not law.
They hold real stocks — bought at prices that already assumed the theme wins.

questions.prompt: An investor sells everything during a crash, planning to "get back in when things calm down." The predictable flaw:
options: Brokers prohibit re-buying for five years
The market's best days cluster around its worst — by the time things feel calm, the violent rebound has already happened without them
Selling in a crash is impossible
There is no flaw — this reliably works
feedback: No such restriction exists — the barrier to getting back in is psychological and informational, which is exactly why it fails.
Right — the plan sells the losses at the bottom and then specifically misses the recovery days, which are born inside the panic, not after it. 'Calm' is the all-clear that comes too late.
Selling is all too possible — panics have plenty of liquidity at falling prices; the spread is wider (concept 5), but the real damage is the exit itself.
Study after study finds this the single most expensive pattern in retail investing — it converts a temporary decline into a permanent loss.

questions.prompt: Decades of brokerage-account research on retail trading frequency finds:
options: Frequent traders outperform through practice
The more investors trade, the worse their net results — spreads, taxes, and timing errors compound against activity
Trading frequency has no measurable effect
Only professionals are allowed to trade frequently
feedback: Practice improves skills where feedback is fast and causal — markets give noisy, delayed feedback, and costs are certain while edge is not.
Right — every trade pays a spread, may book a tax, and re-rolls the timing dice. 'Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth' is a research title, not a slogan.
The effect is large, measurable, and one of the most replicated results in household finance — activity predicts underperformance.
Anyone may trade at will — the finding is that most would be richer if they exercised the right far less often.

questions.prompt: The best defense against selling in a panic is:
options: Watching financial news continuously for early warnings
Choosing a stock/bond mix whose worst case you can genuinely sit through, and writing the plan down before the storm
Keeping everything in cash permanently
Planning to sell quickly at the first sign of trouble
feedback: More news flow raises the urge to act — it's an accelerant for panic-selling, not a warning system; crashes aren't announced in advance.
Right — the mix you can hold beats the optimal mix you'll abandon. Decide in peacetime so that in a crash you're complying with a plan, not making one.
Cash can't crash, but it also can't compound — decades of inflation quietly deliver the big permanent loss you were avoiding.
That IS panic-selling, scheduled in advance — 'the first sign of trouble' is indistinguishable from ordinary volatility until too late, and the rebound clusters right behind it.

preface.hook: You can own a tiny slice of five hundred companies at once, for the price of one share, and pay almost nothing for it.
body: Buying shares in one company means your money rides on that company. If it does well you do well. If it burns down, so does your money. Picking the right one is hard — professionals who do it full time mostly do not beat simply owning everything.

So instead, imagine a big shared pot. Thousands of people put money in, and the pot buys a small piece of every large company in the country. You buy a share of the pot. Now you own a sliver of all of them.

That is an index fund. An ETF is one you can buy and sell on the stock market like a single share, at any moment the market is open, rather than posting an order that settles once at the end of the day. It also tends to hand you smaller tax bills along the way, for reasons buried in how new shares of the pot get created. One company going bust barely dents it either way, because it was only ever a fraction of a percent of what you hold.

The other half of the story is cost. Someone picking shares for you charges real money every year — often one or two percent. A pot that simply holds everything needs almost no decisions, so it can charge a tiny fraction of that.

That difference sounds trivial and is not. Over decades, fees compound exactly like returns do, just against you. The unglamorous move — own everything, pay almost nothing, wait a long time — beats most clever ones.

aha.title: Doing nothing is a strategy, and a good one
aha.text: It feels like you ought to be picking, timing, reacting. The evidence is unkind to that instinct. Most of the gain goes to people who bought sensible things and then left them alone for a very long time.

aha.title: Small fees are not small
aha.text: One percent a year sounds like a rounding error. Over forty years it quietly takes about a THIRD of what you would otherwise have had — and that figure barely changes whether markets do well or badly. It is charged either way.

aha.title: Spreading out is not free of risk
aha.text: Owning everything protects you from any single company failing. It does not protect you when the whole market falls at once, which it does, sometimes badly. Diversification handles one kind of danger and not the other.

preface.closer: Own a little of everything, pay almost nothing, and be patient.
